'''''Sicyos angulatus''''',<ref>{{ITIS | id = 22402 | taxon = ''Sicyos angulatus'' | accessdate = October 16, 2007 }}</ref> the '''oneseed bur cucumber'''<ref name=USDA>{{PLANTS|id=SIAN|taxon=Sicyos angulatus|accessdate=12 November 2015}}</ref> or '''star-cucumber''' is an [[annual plant|annual]] [[vine]] in the gourd family, [[Cucurbitaceae]], native to eastern [[North America]]. The plant forms mats or climbs using tendrils. The leaves are palmately veined and lobed, the flowers are green to yellowish green, and the fruits form clusters of very small [[Berry (botany)#Modified berries|pepos]].

==Description==
The vine produces long branching annual stems that climb over shrubs and fences or trail across the ground. The stems are hairy, pale green and furrowed. The alternate leaves have three to five palmate lobes and can be {{convert|8|in|cm|0|abbr=on}} across. The margin is slightly toothed, the upper surface of the blade is usually hairless and the under side has fine hairs, especially on the veins. The [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] is thick and hairy, and about {{convert|5|in|cm|0|abbr=on}} long. The leaf is deeply indented where it is attached to the petiole. Opposite some of the junctions formed by the petiole and stem, grow branched tendrils, and at others there are flower shoots. The plant is [[monoecious]], with separate male and female blooms. The male flowers are in long-stemmed racemes. Each flower is about {{convert|0.3|in|cm|1|abbr=on}} wide, with a calyx with five pointed teeth, a whitish, green-veined corolla with five lobes, and a central boss of stamens. The small female flowers are bunched together on a short stalk, each having its ovary enclosed in a spiny, hairy fruit; one seed is produced by each flower. The fruit, seen in small clusters, is about {{convert|0.5|in|cm|1|abbr=on}} long, green at first but becomes brown with age; it is dispersed by animals which come into contact with its bristly surface.<ref name=Illinois>{{cite web |url=http://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/savanna/plants/bur_cuke.htm |title=Bur cucumber |author=Hilty, John |work=Wildflowers of Illinois: Savannas and Thickets|accessdate=8 December 2016}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''S. angulatus'' is native to [[Ontario]] and [[Quebec]] in Canada, and the eastern and southern parts of the United States as far west as [[North Dakota]] and [[Texas]].<ref name=USDA/> It grows in fertile, moist habitats such as floodplain areas, damp grassland, thickets, bushy places, river banks, ditches and field verges. It appreciates [[disturbed ground]].<ref name=Illinois/>

=== Invasive species ===
[[File:Sicyos angulatus infestation on river Po banks 03.png|thumb|upright|Infestation on the [[River Po]] banks ]]
In Europe the ''oneseed bur cucumber'' was introduced as an [[ornamental plant]] during the 18th century; the first report of its [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalization]] in [[Germany]] dates back to 1835. In Italy, it was reported in [[Trentino]] since 1853.<ref name = "Piem">{{cite web  | language = it | title = Scheda monografica "Sicyos angulatus"  | publisher =  Regione Piemonte | author = Gruppo di Lavoro Specie Esotiche della Regione Piemonte (a cura del) | date = 2015 |  url = https://www.regione.piemonte.it/web/sites/default/files/media/documenti/2020-11/sicyos_angulatus_-_scheda_semplificata.pdf | accessdate = 2020-12-21  }} .</ref> Nowadays ''Sicyos angulatus'' is considered an [[invasive species]], quite difficult to control because its [[seed bank]] can last in the ground for at least three years after the destruction of the aerial part of the plant. Its infestation can be impressive, covering the pre-existing vegetation with thick and heavy mats. The species tend to spread along river banks, where it finds the better ecological conditions for its growth, but recently it can also be found alongside road and field edges.<ref> {{cite web  | language = it | title = Scheda monografica "sicio, zucca matta" |  publisher =  Regione Lombardia | author = Osservatorio regionale della biodversità (a cura del) | url = http://www.biodiversita.lombardia.it/sito/images/ROBERTA/C03_Sycios.pdf | accessdate= 2020-12-21   }}</ref>

==Ecology==
[[Bumblebee]]s and [[honey bee]]s, as well as various [[Fly|flies]], [[Sphecidae|sphecid wasps]] and [[Vespidae|vespid wasps]] are attracted to the [[nectar]] produced by the flowers. Some bees also collect [[pollen]] from the male flowers. ''[[Anasa armigera]]''  (horned squash bug) and ''[[Anasa repetita|A. repetita]]'' feed on the plant, as do the [[spotted cucumber beetle]], the [[striped cucumber beetle]] and the leaf beetle ''[[Acalymma gouldi]]''. Herbivorous mammals seem to avoid the plant.<ref name=Illinois/>

==Uses==
The foliage of ''Sicyos angulatus'' can be cooked and eaten as a green vegetable. A [[decoction]] of the plant is reputed to be used in traditional Native American medicine to treat [[venereal disease]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Sicyos+angulatus |title=''Sicyos angulatus'' - L. |publisher=Plants For A Future |accessdate=13 December 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://naeb.brit.org/uses/37945/ |title=Cucurbitaceae ''Sicyos angulatus'' L. |publisher=Native American Ethnobotany |accessdate=22 December 2016}}</ref>
